notes.heading: Distinguish a gradient from the evidence for a mechanism
paragraphs: Direction alone is not enough unless the relevant gradient is specified. Diffusion describes net movement down a concentration gradient for the substance considered, while osmosis describes net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane in terms of water potential. An inhibitor experiment can support a role for cellular energy, but an inhibitor may also damage cells or affect other processes. Include appropriate controls and test membrane integrity before attributing every change to one transport mechanism. A measured zero net flux can coexist with movement in both directions.

questions.prompt: Two idealised cubic cells have side lengths 1 and 2 arbitrary units. Calculate surface-area-to-volume ratios and explain one implication for exchange per unit volume.
questions.answer: The ratios are 6:1 and 3:1. The larger cube has less exchange surface per unit volume.
solution: Use surface area 6l² and volume l³, giving ratio 6/l.
A lower ratio can constrain exchange relative to internal demand; it does not by itself measure actual transport rate.
markingPoints: Explain reduced surface per unit volume without claiming a measured rate.

questions.prompt: In a fictional experiment, solute uptake decreases after an energy-production inhibitor is added. Explain why this alone does not prove the solute normally uses active transport, and propose a useful control.
questions.answer: The inhibitor may damage membranes or affect other processes. Compare with a solvent-only control and assess cell viability or membrane integrity.
solution: Identify an alternative mechanism for reduced uptake.
Keep other conditions the same and check that the cells remain viable.
markingPoints: Include a viability or membrane-integrity check.

questions.prompt: A membrane lets water pass but not a dissolved solute. Side A has higher water potential than side B. State the initial net movement and explain whether individual water molecules can move in the opposite direction.
questions.answer: Net water movement is A to B. Individual molecules move both ways, but more cross toward B initially.
solution: Use the stated water-potential difference rather than guessing from side labels.
Distinguish net movement from individual molecular motion.
